content: The use of an effective contraceptive method is often necessary following an abortion. Insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD) can be performed either immediately after the abortion or at a later time. Immediate IUD insertion is a viable option because the woman is not pregnant, the cervical os is open, which reduces the pain of insertion, and her motivation to use contraception may be high. However, immediate insertion carries certain risks, such as an increased likelihood of spontaneous expulsion of the device. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of IUD insertion immediately after either a spontaneous or induced abortion. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, POPLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, as of January 27, 2014. Investigators were also contacted to identify additional trials. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that had at least one treatment group involving immediate IUD insertion after an induced abortion or curettage for spontaneous abortion. The methodological quality of each study was assessed, and data were extracted. The analysis focused on discontinuation rates due to accidental pregnancy, uterine perforation, IUD expulsion, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, and an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis was performed in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. A total of 12 trials involving 7,119 participants were identified, most of which had a moderate risk of bias. Five trials compared immediate versus delayed IUD insertion. One trial specifically examined the Copper 7 IUD and found that immediate insertion was associated with a significantly higher risk of expulsion compared to delayed insertion (RR 11.98, 95% CI 1.61 to 89.35; 1 study, 259 participants). The quality of evidence for this finding was moderate. Similarly, moderate-quality evidence indicated that both the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) and the CuT380A IUD were more likely to be used and expelled when inserted immediately after abortion compared to delayed insertion (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.24 to 1.58; 3 studies, 878 participants for LNG-IUS; RR 2.64, 95% CI 1.16 to 6.00; 3 studies, 878 participants for CuT380A). Another trial compared the levonorgestrel IUD to the Nova T IUD and found that discontinuation rates due to pregnancy were higher in the Nova T group (mean difference 8.70, 95% CI 3.92 to 13.48; 1 study, 438 participants). The quality of evidence for this finding was also moderate. Seven trials focused exclusively on immediate IUD insertion. A meta-analysis of two multicenter trials showed that the TCu 220C IUD was associated with a lower likelihood of pregnancy compared to the Lippes Loop (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.75; 2 studies, 2,257 participants) and a lower risk of expulsion (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.81; 2 studies, 2,257 participants). When comparing the TCu 220C to the Copper 7 IUD, the TCu 220C was associated with a lower risk of pregnancy (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.77; 2 studies, 2,274 participants) and a lower risk of expulsion (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.91; 2 studies, 2,274 participants). Additionally, adding copper sleeves to the Lippes Loop improved its efficacy (RR 3.40, 95% CI 1.28 to 9.04; 1 study, 400 participants) and reduced the risk of expulsion (RR 3.00, 95% CI 1.51 to 5.97; 1 study, 400 participants). In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence supports the safety and practicality of immediate IUD insertion following an abortion. While the risk of IUD expulsion is higher with immediate insertion compared to delayed insertion, the overall use of IUDs at six months post-abortion is higher when the device is inserted immediately.
